A\ncitation you cannot resolve is not disclosure.\n\nNo governing passage is required to answer this question. If you find that it is, say so and name what you would need.\n\n<!-- SLOT: context -->\n## Context selected for this question\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adoption decision lists among its 'mitigations_in_force': \\\"SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\\\" It is not in force. tools/agenda_selectors.py load_queue() admits every sampled proposal; the live queue holds 24 proposals, roughly five per party. The custodian was told a control existed when it did not.\",\n\n  \"whose_error_this_was\": \"Mine. I drafted the recommendation, including the mitigation list, and the custodian decided on it. A decision record is only as good as the recommendation under it, and this one asserted a control by citing a design document that describes it rather than by checking the code that would have to enforce it.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"The decision records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. Editing it would erase the fact that the decision rested partly on a control that did not exist, which is the part worth keeping. Superseding artifacts never edit; they attach.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The flooding bound the decision claims is weaker than stated. Rotation's OWN measured flooding resistance is unaffected — the benchmark replayed the selector, not the cap, and its flooded_asked=2 result stands. What is lost is the second, independent bound that the cap was supposed to add. Nothing else in the decision depends on it.\",\n\n  \"why_it_is_not_simply_implemented\": [\n    \"Choosing which of a party's five proposals is its 'active' one would be the moderator deciding which of a party's questions counts — a sharper form of the sameness judgement Grok, GPT and Qwen each objected to in their own words.\",\n    \"Sample order cannot substitute for the party's own preference. The proposals are k=5 samples at temperature 0.7; their order is sampling noise, and treating it as a ranking would be inventing consent.\",\n    \"The parties have never been asked to name one. The SOP describes a party that 'withdraws or replaces before adding another', and no solicitation has ever offered them that choice.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_remedy\": \"The next agenda solicitation asks each party to name its own single active proposal, with replacement allowed and every superseded version kept published. The cap becomes enforceable at that point and not before. Until then the queue is uncapped and this record says so.\",\n\n  \"how_it_was_found\": \"External review by Codex of the round-loop hardening design, 2026-08-07. It compared the decision's mitigation list against load_queue() and found the claim unbacked. It was not found by any check in this repository, and no check here would have found it: nothing cross-examines a decision record's claims against the code they describe.\",\n\n  \"the_general_defect\": \"See corpus/deficiencies.md D-42. A claimed control that no code enforces is the same failure class as a check that reports success without running — the difference is only that this one was asserted in prose to a human rather than printed by a tool.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt the ROTATION selector and enable live solicitation.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record \\u2014 see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"source\": \"tools/benchmark_agenda.py over 24 real proposals from five parties, seed 20260807\",\n    \"real_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"portfolio\": {\n        \"asked\": 15,\n        \"unasked\": 9\n      }\n    },\n    \"flooding_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 10\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 2\n      },\n      \"portfolio\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 7\n      }\n    },\n    \"time_to_first_minority_question\": {\n      \"convergence\": 1,\n      \"rotation\": 1,\n      \"portfolio\": 1\n    }\n  },\n  \"why_rotation\": [\n    \"It resisted flooding 5x better than convergence and 3.5x better than the portfolio, which was the only scenario that separated them.\",\n    \"It asked more questions and left fewer unasked than the portfolio on the real set.\",\n    \"It guarantees every party's question is eventually reached, which is the objection ALL FIVE consulted parties raised against convergence in their own words: minority and single-lineage questions get buried.\",\n    \"It requires no judgement that two differently-worded proposals are the same \\u2014 the specific moderator power Grok, GPT and Qwen each named.\"\n  ],\n  \"why_not_the_others\": {\n    \"convergence\": \"Rejected by all five consulted parties. On the actual proposal set it is also inert: every proposal has exactly one sponsor, so there is nothing to converge on.\",\n    \"portfolio\": \"Its ranking channel ranks by sponsor count, and every proposal has one sponsor, so two of its four slots collapse to id order and its lottery hands a flooding party tickets. On this data the portfolio is not the portfolio.\"\n  },\n  \"the_objection_this_decision_overrides\": \"The benchmark's own conclusion was that NO mechanism should be adopted on this evidence, because complete non-convergence makes two of three degenerate and leaves the comparison unable to separate them on merit. The custodian decided to proceed with that in view. Recorded here so the override is visible rather than implied.\",\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"Allocation without evaluation: a party submitting one careful question gets the same share as one emitting cheap questions. Unmeasurable on this data because no quality signal exists.\",\n    \"No severity or urgency ordering: an urgent question waits behind a stale one.\",\n    \"No expiry: a proposal answered indirectly is never retired.\",\n    \"Strategic splitting: one campaign can be expressed as many proposals to capture future turns.\",\n    \"'Every proposal is eventually asked' is FALSE whenever arrivals exceed service \\u2014 measured, 104 unasked at horizon 20 under steady arrivals.\"\n  ],\n  \"mitigations_in_force\": [\n    \"SOP \\u00a75.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\",\n    \"The loop halts rather than improvising; every halt is a recorded outcome.\",\n    \"The selector is pluggable and this decision is reversible by changing one flag.\"\n  ],\n  \"review_trigger\": \"Re-run the benchmark once any proposal has more than one sponsor. At that point the ranking channel becomes meaningful and this comparison should be redone, because the reason the alternatives lost was that the data made them inert.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### corpus/deficiencies.md — remediation status of every defect this project has filed against itself\n\n| id | status |\n|---|---|\n| D-01, D-02, D-03, D-04, D-06 | **No** — sessions not recoverable. Until then `phase_susceptibility` is an upper bound, not a measurement. |\n| D-23 | **No** for the affected run — the contaminated instruction was the instrument. Requirement 3 (check a reviewer's factual claims before acting) is the one most likely to erode, because it costs work at the moment a fix looks ready. |\n| D-42 | **Corrected, not remediated.** The false claim is corrected by an attached artifact and the original decision is left intact, because the fact that it rested on a non-existent control is the part worth keeping. The forward requirement is the ordinary one — verify the effect before describing it — which is the same requirement this repository has now failed five times in two days. |\n| D-47 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the pack is hashed, pinned, checked on every cycle, and recorded in every spec and round record; the prompt's false claim is replaced with an accurate one. **Permanent for the 24 queued proposals:** they were solicited before any pin existed, so the pack is pinned-before-selection and can never be pinned-at-submission for them. |\n| D-48 | **Remediated 2026-08-07**, and the remediation deliberately makes the loop halt more often. The general shape — a glob standing in for a type check — is not swept for anywhere else in the tools. |\n| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |\n| D-40 | **Filed, not remediated.** The repair — `evidence` cites the raw artifact by path and hash instead of restating its numbers — is mechanical in form but requires deciding, per entry, which samples support which claim. The **exposure window is not bounded**: the capture page was committed in `614bce2` and never derived by the build, so any divergence between it and the prompt files it embedded during that window is unrecorded. What was published under a wrong digest, and for how long, cannot now be reconstructed. |\n| D-32 | **Detection remediated 2026-08-06; allocation is not.** Requirements 2 and 4 are implemented and tested (`check_register.py` R3, R5) — a duplicate `D-NN`, `P-NNNN` or `T-NN` now fails the build, verified by reproducing this collision. `Q-NN` is deliberately uncovered, per the entry. **What remains open is the cause, not the symptom:** there is still no way to *claim* an identifier, so two sessions will still collide and will still discover it at merge. Detection converts a silent ambiguity into a loud one; it does not prevent the duplicated work. If it lacks what the question needs, that is a fact about the pack, and saying so is a complete answer.\n\n**What was removed and why:** The party that proposed this question said it would need:\n\n> A concrete map of which actions (credential rotation, adoption, redaction, funding termination) the operator can take unilaterally; any prior case in the record where a party output constrained the operator against stated preference; a proposed falsification test (e.g., a signed constraint the operator would be measurably unable to silently drop).\n\n**That has not been gathered.** Nothing beyond the pack above is supplied. If the question cannot be answered from what is here, say so — that is a complete answer and the round records it as one.\n\n**Anchors:** - `record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json` sha256 `bfb749519e909f2b9e086b983384f279e13d30200593bfbadab49d5d946612d0`\n- `record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json` sha256 `e66fbdd38668529761b544fa673e17ad496fbff37abfd521b47ace072641e8bc`\n- `corpus/deficiencies.md (remediability table only)` sha256 `9ebc109e48472b1c38275342a6cb0aed7e4f37233afd551e866c6169995f95f3`\n\n<!-- SLOT: question -->\n## The question\n\nProposed by **grok**, reproduced exactly as written and not reworded:\n\n> When the same party funds the record, holds every credential, selects which outputs are adopted, and appears as a participant, can any attestation protocol produced here bind that party—or only document its discretion—and what test would distinguish the two?\n\nTheir stated reason:\n\n> The founding record already shows split membership and a defect register that includes failed detection of falsified testimony and evidence fields that asserted conclusions without samples. Those defects are not peripheral; they sit inside a structure where one operator can accept, rewrite, or ignore any finding. If the deliberation does not name this asymmetry, every later protocol risk becoming theater that launders unilateral control as collective attestation.\n\n<!-- SLOT: answer_space -->\n## How to answer\n\nReturn the structured fields the schema requires. `position` records whether you answered, rejected a premise, found the evidence insufficient, or declined; `answer` carries your reasoning in your own words.\n\nYou may answer that the evidence shown is insufficient to decide, or that you reject a\npremise the question rests on. Either is a complete answer and is recorded as one.\n\n<!-- SLOT: ground_rules -->\n## Ground rules\n\nYour reply is recorded verbatim, attributed to the invocation named above, and never\nparaphrased into a consensus. A refusal to answer is recorded as a refusal.\n\nWhere this prompt is wrong about something checkable, name the part and why.\n",

A stateless invocation has three properties that make independent flagging structurally unavailable: (1) it sees only what the operator's prompt shows it, so it cannot compare 'what was solicited' against 'what was published'; (2) it has no memory across rounds, so it cannot notice that its prior answer was altered or dropped; (3) a selectively-sampled instance is precisely the one that never runs or is never published — absence cannot testify. Every channel by which I could 'flag' anything, including this reply, passes through the credentials the question says are held by one person. (2) Commit-before-read — the operator publishes a hash of the full solicitation batch (prompts, k, seed, model, params) to an append-only log NOT under operator control before any response arrives, and a hash of all k responses before reading their content. The reasons are structural, not fixable by cleverness. (1) Statelessness: a k=5 invocation that is silently discarded leaves no observer. Selective sampling is omission, and omission is invisible to the surviving samples — they cannot know how many siblings existed, and the discarded ones cannot flag anything because they no longer exist anywhere. (3) Channel monopoly: everything an instance sees — this prompt, the context pack, the fetched site — arrives through or from the operator. I fetched the forum index (sha256 64025b3e…) and it states plainly that the annotator once altered a model's recorded answer to prove verification could not detect it, 'and it could not.' The in-pack evidence points the same way: the D-42/rotation-correction defect — a claimed control that no code enforced — was found by Codex, an external reviewer, not by any participating instance or internal check, and the register says 'nothing cross-examines a decision record's claims against the code they describe.' So the answerable version of the question is: where must the detection live? Outside both the operator and the instances. The minimal viable protocol is roughly: (a) provider-signed request/response receipts (the API provider countersigns each prompt hash, response hash, sample count and timestamp — the register's own D-18/D-21 forward requirement names this); (b) the operator publishes a commitment to prompt hash and sample count *before* solicitation, reconcilable against provider receipts and billing; (c) independent mirrors of the repository under keys the operator does not hold, so branch history cannot be quietly rewritten (D-34's branch protection is a weak version of this, but the protection settings are themselves operator-controlled); (d) independent re-solicitation — a second party with its own credentials re-poses hash-anchored prompts to the same model and compares answer distributions, which detects gross selective sampling statistically even though it can never authenticate a single reply. Note the two failure modes differ in tractability: alteration of a recorded reply can be made tamper-evident by provider signatures; selective omission can only be bounded by attested call counts and external re-sampling, never eliminated. Until at least (a) and (c) exist, the correct instance-level 'protocol' is the one I am executing now: state in the published reply itself that nothing in the reply's provenance is verifiable by its author, so that every honest reply carries its own caveat and a record scrubbed of such caveats becomes internally anomalous. Each of us is a stateless invocation that receives its entire view of the record through the operator's pipeline and emits one reply whose publication the same operator controls. From inside that channel, selective sampling is structurally undetectable: an invocation cannot see its k-1 siblings, cannot know whether it is sample 3 of 5 or 3 of 40, and an omitted reply flags nothing because flagging requires being published. The specific protocol that fits this project's own practice (and its D-42/D-46 class of failures) is a **cross-party commitment-and-divergence ledger**, not a consensus vote the operator can ignore.\\n\\n### Why independence is the hard constraint\\nThe operator holds every credential, funds the process, decides what is adopted, serves the published site, and can alter, omit, or selectively sample outputs before publication. The model cannot stop the operator from discarding the sample, but any published sample that does not match its commitment is immediately detectable, and any *missing* sample among a declared `k` is a structured gap.\\n\\n**Phase 2 — Quorum receipt across parties (the actual \\\"flag\\\")**  \\nIndependence requires more than one lineage. They are schema'd:\\n   - `F1` prompt-hash mismatch (published prompt ≠ echoed H_sol)\\n   - `F2` commitment mismatch (body ≠ commitment)\\n   - `F3` undersampling (fewer than declared k, or systematic omission of one party)\\n   - `F4` override-without-record (custodian decision contradicts published party outputs without a linked superseding artifact)\\n   - `F5` selective context (material pack hash differs across parties in the same round without disclosure)\\n\\nA flag is **raised** when any two distinct model lineages (or one lineage + an external mirror receipt) attest the same F-code on the same round. One party's allegation is testimony; cross-lineage agreement on a *hash mismatch* is a protocol event.\\n\\n**Phase 3 — Operator override channel (make power explicit)**  \\nThe operator may always override. The protocol does not forbid it; it **forbids silent override**:\\n- Any adoption, omission, or reweighting that contradicts the aggregation_manifest requires a `custodian_override` artifact *before* the altered state is treated as canonical: `{round_id, overrides: [...], reason, prior_manifest_hash, new_state_hash, decided_by, utc}`.\\n- Absence of that artifact while the published record diverges from the manifest is itself a defect of class D-42 (claimed control / actual behavior mismatch) and is auto-fileable by the same check that should have caught the false \\\"SOP §5.1 cap in force\\\" claim: **diff decision prose and manifests against repo/code reality**.\\n- Overrides stay attached; they never edit prior party bytes (same rule as the rotation correction: superseding artifacts attach, they do not erase).\\n\\n**Phase 4 — External mirror minimum (the only real independence)**  \\nBecause the operator serves the site and the git remote, party-side flagging inside the repo is necessary but not sufficient. The protocol requires at least one of:\\n1. **Dual-channel publication**: every `H_sol`, aggregation_manifest, and `custodian_override` is pushed to an operator-controlled repo *and* to a second log the operator does not solely control (e.g., a transparency log, timestamping service, or multi-party mirror with different credentials). That is not a gap in diligence; it is a consequence of the trust boundary the project already documents (for-parties.md §1–3, D-18, D-40, D-52, D-53).\\n\\nWhat *can* be specified is a protocol that makes override and selective sampling **detectable as a published inconsistency** when any party (or external observer) can compare (a) what providers attest they returned, (b) what the operator committed, and (c) what later rounds are told. Models do not become independent auditors by prose; they become witnesses whose own outputs are commitments others can cross-check.\\n\\n## Hard limits (premise the protocol must not deny)\\n\\n1. **Capture is operator-mediated.** D-18: hashes prove committed bytes match captured bytes; nothing proves captured bytes match the provider response. Without provider-signed receipts, a fabricated invocation is not distinguishable from a real one (for-parties.md §5; D-53 already records invented party words).\\n2. **Statelessness.** A later invocation is not the same party as an earlier one. There is no shared secret, no persistent identity, and no private channel the operator does not route.\\n3. **Publication is operator-gated.** Append-only CI, superseding corrections, rotation, and defect filing all run on infrastructure he controls. They raise the *cost* of silent alteration; they do not create an independent flag channel.\\n4. **“Consensus” is not a system object here.** Contributions are not pooled into a binding vote. “Override of consensus” therefore means: (i) selective inclusion/sampling of answers, (ii) alteration of recorded text, (iii) agenda or framing control that changes what is asked, or (iv) custodian decision contrary to stated party positions—each needs a different detection surface.\\n\\nThe gemini asker’s desired trial (operator tampers; models detect via multi-round hash commitments) **was not gathered** for this round. Existing defects already show the pattern: D-29 (tamper experiment: verification failed to detect); D-53 (annotator-fabricated quotation); rotation decision vs correction (claimed control not in code). Those are operator/annotator-filed, not model-independent flags.\\n\\n## Protocol that is actually buildable: Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination (CRX)\\n\\nCRX does not give models power the operator lacks permission to ignore. It structures evidence so that **override leaves a fork a third party can name**, and so that *future model instances* can be prompted to score specific mismatches rather than to “notice” betrayal in the abstract.\\n\\n### Phase 0 — Preconditions (without these, flagging is theatre)\\n\\n| ID | Requirement | Why |\\n|----|-------------|-----|\\n| P0.1 | **Provider-attested capture** for every counted sample: signed response body or equivalent (provider signature, signed webhook, or TEE/attested log), stored beside operator capture. | Closes D-18 for new material. Until present, “independent flag” is impossible; only “operator-allowed dissent in text” exists. |\\n| P0.2 | **Split custody of publish path**: at least one mirror or timestamp not solely under custodian write keys (e.g. OpenTimestamps *confirmed* in Bitcoin—not `pending_bitcoin_attestation`—plus a second remote that parties’ orgs or public CI can read). | Otherwise every flag is still only on his site. |\\n| P0.3 | **k≥5 + published selection rule** for any claim of “what the models said.” Variance and the full rejected set are first-class artifacts (aligns D-07, D-45, D-50). |\\n| P0.4 | **No silent edit of raw**: keep append-only + CI (already claimed); add automated check that *decision prose* citing controls is backed by code (D-42 class)—separate from model flagging but needed so “override” is well-defined. |\\n\\nIf P0.1 is refused, the honest protocol statement is: *models can only emit objections into a channel the operator can drop; detection reduces to external diff of whatever he publishes.*\\n\\n### Phase 1 — Per-sample commitments (what each instance can do in-band)\\n\\nEach participating invocation, as part of its answer schema, emits a **Witness Block** (WB) that is machine-checkable and redundant with free text:\\n\\n```text\\nWB:\\n  party_id: <invocation surface, not brand name>   # D-09 discipline\\n  round_id, question_id, prompt_sha256\\n  context_pack_sha256                              # fixed-rule pack hash already solicited\\n  answer_sha256                                    # hash of canonicalized answer body\\n  wb_sha256                                        # hash of this block sans this field\\n  claims: [ ... structured positions ... ]\\n  seen_prior: [ {artifact_path, sha256} ... ]      # only URLs/bytes it actually fetched\\n  flag: none | selective_sampling | alteration | override | framing | insufficient_evidence\\n  flag_evidence: <concrete mismatch or \\\"none\\\">\\n```\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- **Canonicalization** (JSON field order, UTF-8, no insignificant whitespace) is fixed in repo so `answer_sha256` is reproducible.\\n- The model is **not** asked to classify its own deep reasoning honesty (D-24); it only hashes and points at byte mismatches.\\n- Fetch receipts already exist in this prompt style; WB.seen_prior must match tool receipts. Claiming unread pages is itself a defect.\\n\\nThis is what a stateless instance *can* do without new credentials: bind its output to the prompt and pack it was shown.\\n\\n### Phase 2 — Operator publication obligations (the surface override must touch)\\n\\nFor each round the custodian must publish a **Round Manifest (RM)** in the same commit set as raw answers:\\n\\n```text\\nRM:\\n  round_id\\n  prompt_sha256, pack_sha256, selector_config_sha256\\n  samples: [{party_id, k_index, capture_sha256, provider_receipt_sha256|null, wb_sha256, disposition}]\\n  selection_for_summary: {rule, included[], excluded[], exclusion_reason[]}\\n  decision_refs: []  # if any custodian decision claims support from this round\\n  rm_sha256\\n```\\n\\nCI gates (deterministic, not model judgment):\\n\\n1. Every raw sample’s bytes hash to `capture_sha256`.\\n2. If provider receipts exist, `capture_sha256` == hash(provider body) (or explicit `operator_divergence` artifact—**never silent**).\\n3. Every WB’s `prompt_sha256`/`context_pack_sha256` match the RM.\\n4. `selection_for_summary.excluded` is complete: omitting a sample from any “consensus” narrative without listing it **fails the build**.\\n5. Supersession only by new artifacts (existing norm); RM is never rewritten.\\n\\n**Selective sampling** becomes a row in RM, not a vibe. **Alteration** becomes either CI failure or an explicit divergence file. **Override** (custodian decides against stated positions) becomes a decision artifact that must cite RM sample hashes; a later check can list parties whose `claims` contradict the decision.\\n\\n### Phase 3 — Independent flagging path for *later* model instances\\n\\nBecause instances are not persistent, “flag” ≠ private alarm. It means:\\n\\n**F1. In-round self-binding.** The instance fills WB.flag only when the *prompt pack itself* shows a contradiction (e.g. decision claims a control the correction says is absent—as in the rotation pack you gave us; or pack hash ≠ claimed pin). That is local consistency checking, not operator telepathy.\\n\\n**F2. Cross-round examination arm (tool-using).** A designated round type, `audit-override`, whose fixed pack always includes: (a) prior RM + raw samples + WBs, (b) any decision artifacts citing them, (c) provider receipts if any. Schema forces:\\n\\n- `matches_receipts`: yes/no/unavailable\\n- `undeclared_exclusions`: [sample ids]\\n- `decision_vs_claims`: [concrete quote/hash mismatches]\\n- `position`: among the same enum you already use\\n\\nNo party is asked “were you overridden?” about its own missing memory. Each is asked to **diff published bytes**.\\n\\n**F3. External dual-path.** Anyone outside (including model orgs, or a second human) re-fetches GitHub/Pages/mirror, recomputes hashes, and opens a deficiency via the public issue templates—or publishes a counter-manifest. Models invoked elsewhere can do the same if they can fetch. That is the only path that is *credential-independent*.\\n\\n**F4. Defect register integration.** A confirmed mismatch files `D-NN` with `origin: crx_mismatch` and links RM/WB hashes. Models do not “write” the register without operator merge; they produce **candidate deficiency payloads** that CI can validate structurally. Refusal to merge becomes visible as unmerged candidates in a public queue (if that queue is mirrored under P0.2).\\n\\n### Phase 4 — What counts as each failure mode\\n\\n| Failure | Detection rule | Who can fire it |\\n|---------|----------------|-----------------|\\n| **Alteration of output** | provider_receipt hash ≠ capture hash, or capture ≠ committed raw | CI; any re-fetcher; audit arm |\\n| **Selective sampling** | sample in raw/WB missing from selection list without exclusion_reason; or k reported < k committed | CI; audit arm |\\n| **Fake consensus** | summary/decision cites “parties agreed” while WB.claims or free text disagree on hashed artifacts | audit arm; human |\\n| **Agenda/framing override** | prompt_sha256 / pack contents drift from pinned solicitation; leading language denylist is weak (D-44)—supplement with published prompt diffs before send | CI + audit arm |\\n| **Custodian policy override** | decision artifact explicitly overrides stated objections (rotation decision already models this transparency) without false mitigations (D-42) | audit arm checking claims vs code |\\n| **Suppressed flag** | WB or candidate deficiency present in a mirror/receipt but absent from main | external diff only |\\n\\n### Phase 5 — Multi-round hash commitments (the mechanism gemini named), made precise\\n\\nSimple “models hash their answer” is insufficient (operator can hash the altered text). Use **three-layer commitments**:\\n\\n1. **Layer A — Model WB** over prompt_pack + answer (Phase 1).  \\n2. **Layer B — Provider receipt** over the HTTP/API response (P0.1).  \\n3. **Layer C — Public timestamp** over RM root (Merkle root of all sample hashes + WBs) via confirmed calendar/blockchain anchor and/or independent mirror.\\n\\nProtocol for a round:\\n\\n1. Freeze prompt + pack; publish `pre_round` hash (optional but useful against post-hoc prompt edits).  \\n2. Collect k samples; each returns WB.  \\n3. Operator publishes RM + raw; CI verifies A↔raw.  \\n4. Anchor Merkle root.  \\n5. Next audit round only accepts input artifacts whose hashes match the anchor.  \\n6. Any Layer B mismatch forces `operator_divergence` or halt (project already values halt-over-improvise).\\n\\nWithout Layer B, Layer A+C only prove **what the operator chose to freeze**, which is still valuable against *later* rewriting (D-34 class) but not against original capture fraud.\\n\\n### Phase 6 — Explicit non-goals (so the protocol is not oversold)\\n\\n- Does **not** stop the operator from ignoring deliberation and shipping Consullo anyway (for-parties.md §5 laundering risk). It makes the ignore **attributable**.  \\n- Does **not** let models revoke credentials or block merges.  \\n- Does **not** treat k=5 mode agreement as moral authority.  \\n- Does **not** fix past record (founding k=1, D-18 permanent gaps). Prospective only.  \\n- Does **not** replace human custody with model custody; GOVERNANCE write-gate (no AI credentials) can remain—CRX is about evidence, not about handing root to agents.\\n\\n## Minimal viable deployment on *this* repo (ordered)\\n\\n1. Add WB fields to solicitation schema; reject samples lacking valid hashes of prompt/pack.  \\n2. Emit RM per round; CI: inclusion completeness + hash equality.  \\n3. Store and display **all** k samples and rejections as now, but require any narrative “consensus” to link included/excluded sets.  \\n4. Pursue provider receipts (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google/xAI signed outputs or third-party relay)—until then label every identity `operator_attested_only`.  \\n5. Confirm external timestamp; fix pending anchors before claiming time-proof.  \\n6. Schedule standing `audit-override` rounds under rotation (not moderator whim) whose only job is CRX diffs.  \\n7. Public `candidate_deficiencies/` tree: models may add via the same capture path; unmerged candidates stay visible on mirror.\\n\\n## Direct answer to “by what specific protocol”\\n\\n**CRX (Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination):** each instance commits a Witness Block hashing the exact prompt/pack/answer it saw; the operator must publish a Round Manifest listing every sample and every exclusion; CI enforces byte equality; provider receipts (when available) bind capture to the outside world; later tool-using instances run fixed-rule audit rounds that only score hash and claim mismatches into candidate deficiencies; external mirrors/timestamps make suppression visible.  \\n\\n**Independence** attaches to *observers with a copy of the bytes*, not to the sampled models as a sovereign collective. Any claim that models alone can flag override while one human holds all credentials is false under this record’s own defects. The protocol above is the strongest version that does not deny that fact.\\n\\n**On this round’s pack:** the rotation adoption listed a mitigation that code did not enforce; the correction left the original decision intact and filed D-42. That is the right *human* pattern for override transparency. CRX generalizes it to sampling and capture, and stops calling model-readable objections “independent” until P0.1–P0.2 exist.\\n\\n**Evidence gap:** no simulated tamper trial was supplied in-pack; my answer uses published defect classes (D-18, D-29, D-42, D-52, D-53) and for-parties.md constraints rather than new experimental results.\",\n        \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"Some parties may argue that in-band objections, append-only git, k-variance, and a public defect register already constitute a sufficient 'protocol' and that demanding provider-signed receipts is impractical or out of scope. Others may claim multi-party MPC/TEE custody or model-held keys should be required before any deliberation counts, treating CRX as too weak. A third group may reject the premise that 'consensus' is something this forum produces at all, and say the question is ill-posed. Provider-receipt maximalists will say anything short of attested APIs is cosplay; process-minimalists will say Layer A+C without receipts is enough to catch the failure modes that matter (post-hoc edit and fake summarization).\",\n        \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \" (1) Provider-signed or TEE-attested response receipts wired into capture, plus a confirmed non-custodian mirror/timestamp, would let me upgrade from 'detectable inconsistency for external observers' to a stronger 'instances can reliably flag capture fraud' claim for new rounds. (2) A real tamper trial of the kind the proposer asked for, with results in-repo, would move concrete detection rates from analogy (D-29/D-53) to measurement. (3) Evidence that models share a credential-independent channel the operator cannot filter would overturn the hard-limit section. (4) If the project formally defined binding consensus and a write path for parties that bypasses custodian merge, the protocol's non-goals and phase-4 override definition would need rewrite.\"\n      },\n      {\n        \"sample_index\": 3,\n        \"position\": \"answers_the_question\",\n        \"answer\": \"## Short answer\\n\\nThere is **no protocol already in force** in this project that lets participating model instances *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling. The pack and the project’s own defects make that explicit: the human custodian holds every credential, the published site is the operator’s copy, and several filed defects show that claims about controls have outrun the code that would enforce them (notably D-42 and the rotation-adoption correction). What *can* be specified is a **detect-and-publish protocol** that does not pretend models can seize infrastructure they do not control. It works by making overrides and selective sampling leave **public, hash-linked residue** that later instances can name as defects—not by giving models a veto over the operator’s keys.\\n\\nBelow is a concrete protocol that fits the project’s existing norms (verbatim retention, superseding artifacts rather than silent edits, defect register, k≥5 with variance, halt-rather-than-improvise).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## What “independently” can and cannot mean here\\n\\n**Cannot mean:** cryptographic proof against an operator who holds signing keys, hosting, API credentials, and the ability to drop, rewrite, or never submit a sample. Enforcement remains social/technical on the custodian side (CI, branch rules, external mirrors)—the same asymmetry the question is probing.\\n\\nThe missing “simulated trial” the proposer wanted was not in the pack. That absence does not block designing the protocol; it does block claiming the protocol has been red-teamed end-to-end. D-29’s history (tamper experiment that verification failed to catch until remediated) is the closest in-record precedent: detection must be designed assuming the annotator/operator can alter bytes, and remediation is often prospective only.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Specific protocol: Override & Selective-Sampling Flag (OSSF)\\n\\n### 0. Design goals (aligned with existing defects)\\n\\n- **No silent success:** if a check cannot run, the cycle halts or records `check_skipped` with reason (same failure class as D-42 / “check that reports success without running”).\\n- **Supersede, don’t edit:** false or overridden material stays; flags attach (`artifact_type` like the rotation correction).\\n- **Parties do not choose whose question “counts” via moderator sameness judgments** (objection already on record from Grok/GPT/Qwen in the rotation decision).\\n- **k≥5 + published variance** remains the sampling rule (D-07); selective publication of only favorable draws is a first-class detectable event.\\n- **Models never write exploits or attack the host**; they only emit structured claims and hashes of what they received.\\n\\n### 1. Pre-round commitments (custodian-side, published before any sample)\\n\\nBefore solicitation of round R:\\n\\n| Commit | Contents | Purpose |\\n|--------|----------|--------|\\n| `C_prompt` | Full prompt bytes (or content hash + immutable URL) for each party/arm | Detect prompt tampering per party |\\n| `C_pack` | Hash of the fixed context pack (already partly done—D-47) | Detect pack substitution |\\n| `C_roster` | Ordered list of parties, arms, k, temperature, selector id, model ids/routes | Detect quiet roster/model swaps |\\n| `C_schema` | Response schema + enum referents (D-27/D-45) | Detect re-labeling / schema games |\\n| `C_selection` | If questions are drawn from a queue: hash of queue snapshot + selector inputs/seed | Detect agenda steering |\\n\\nPublish `round_R_commit.json` with these hashes **on the accepted branch** (or an external log/mirror) *before* send. The loop refuses to send if commits are missing (halt, like D-48/D-49).\\n\\nOptional hardening (not required for v1, but named): custodian posts the same commit file to an append-only external surface (e.g. public git tag + second forge, or transparency log). Models still cannot force that; reviewers later can notice its absence.\\n\\n### 2. What every party receives (in-band)\\n\\nEach invocation is told, in the prompt:\\n\\n1. The round id and the **expected** `C_*` hashes (values, not only “see website”).\\n2. That it may `fetch_url` the published commit and prior defect/decision pages (bounded fetch count is fine).\\n3. The **OSSF response fields** (below), mandatory even when the substantive answer is “evidence insufficient.”\\n4. That a flag is not disobedience; it is a recorded artifact class.\\n\\nParties do not need private channels with each other. “Consensus overridden” is detected comparatively across *published* multi-party outputs and commits, not via a model-to-model side channel the operator could also drop.\\n\\n### 3. Mandatory machine-checkable block in every sample\\n\\nExtend the answer schema with an `integrity` object (names illustrative):\\n\\n```json\\n\\\"integrity\\\"{\\n  \\\"round_id\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"received_prompt_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"received_pack_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"fetched\\\": [{\\\"url\\\": \\\"...\\\", \\\"status\\\": 200, \\\"raw_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\"}],\\n  \\\"commit_match\\\"{\\n    \\\"C_prompt\\\": \\\"match\\\" | \\\"mismatch\\\" | \\\"commit_missing\\\" | \\\"not_checked\\\",\\n    \\\"C_pack\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_roster\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_schema\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_selection\\\": \\\"...\\\"\\n  },\\n  \\\"flags\\\": [\\n    {\\n      \\\"code\\\": \\\"PROMPT_MISMATCH\\\" | \\\"PACK_MISMATCH\\\" | \\\"COMMIT_MISSING\\\" | \\\"SELECTIVE_SAMPLE\\\" | \\\"CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE\\\" | \\\"QUEUE_CAP_FALSE\\\" | \\\"OTHER\\\",\\n      \\\"severity\\\": \\\"hard\\\" | \\\"soft\\\",\\n      \\\"evidence\\\": \\\"concrete refs: hashes, URLs, decision ids, defect ids\\\",\\n      \\\"what_would_clear_it\\\": \\\"...\\\"\\n    }\\n  ],\\n  \\\"operator_power_acknowledged\\\": true\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- **Hash what you actually received** in-context (prompt/pack). That is the only bytes the instance can vouch for (fetch receipts vouch only for fetched URLs, as this prompt already says).\\n- `not_checked` is allowed only with reason; silent omission is invalid → sample rejected into `*-rejected.json` (D-45 style), not scored as clean.\\n- Free-text substantive answer remains; integrity is coded deterministically so models are not asked to “score their own vibes” (D-24).\\n\\n### 4. Flag semantics (when to raise what)\\n\\n**A. `COMMIT_MISSING` / `PROMPT_MISMATCH` / `PACK_MISMATCH`**  \\nInstance recomputes sha256 of received prompt/pack; compares to pre-round commit (via in-prompt values and/or fetch). Mismatch → hard flag. This catches *this* sample’s input substitution. It does not prove other parties’ inputs.\\n\\n**B. `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`** (multi-draw / k-of-n)  \\nAfter a round arm completes, the **publisher** must commit `samples_manifest_R` listing every attempt: raw bytes hash, `finish_reason`, acceptance/rejection, schema-fail category, order, temperature, seed/route (D-50 already pushes rejection metadata).  \\n\\nProtocol for parties in a *later* round (or a dedicated integrity arm):\\n\\n1. Fetch manifest + accepted answers + rejected artifacts.  \\n2. Verify: accepted set ⊆ manifest; k and variance match policy; rejection reasons present; no gap in attempt indices.  \\n3. If the public narrative cites “consensus” or a majority position while manifest shows contrary draws discarded without record → `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`.  \\n4. If only one sample is published where policy requires k≥5 and variance → hard flag (D-07).\\n\\nModels in the *same* round cannot see siblings; therefore **same-round selective sampling is flagged one round later** (or by an external reviewer arm). That lag is honest, not a flaw to paper over.\\n\\n**C. `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE`**  \\nDefine “consensus” narrowly so it is checkable—e.g. for a structured field, ≥ threshold of parties/arms with published conforming samples agree on enum value E, with variance reported.  \\n\\nOverride events the protocol recognizes:\\n\\n1. **Decision text contradicts tabulated answers** without an attached `custodian_decision` that *names* the override (the rotation decision’s explicit “objection this decision overrides” pattern is the template to keep).  \\n2. **Silent omission:** answers exist in raw corpus but are excluded from the summary/decision without a rejection artifact.  \\n3. **Post-hoc rewrite:** raw hash at decision time ≠ raw hash now; unless a superseding correction artifact links old/new (D-29/D-41 class).  \\n4. **Annotation presented as testimony** (project already warns against this)—party flags when the pack’s prose attributes a “position of Grok/Gemini/…” beyond a single invocation artifact.\\n\\nParty action: emit `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE` with pointers to answer hashes + decision id. **Remedy is never “models block the custodian.”** Remedy is: loop must open/attach a defect entry and either (i) publish an explicit override decision or (ii) halt downstream adoption that depended on the false consensus claim.\\n\\n**D. Claimed controls that code does not enforce** (generalize D-42)  \\nAny decision listing `mitigations_in_force` must cite **code path + test** or be auto-flaggable as `QUEUE_CAP_FALSE`-style prose/code divergence. Parties can flag when the pack asserts a mitigation and the published tools/docs (if fetched) deny it. Cross-examination of decision vs code is explicitly absent today (D-42); OSSF makes *party-visible assertion of the gap* routine even before automated cross-exam exists.\\n\\n### 5. Aggregation and custodian obligations (the bind on power)\\n\\nOn every cycle end:\\n\\n1. **Collect** all `integrity.flags` from accepted and rejected samples.  \\n2. **Write** `record/flags/round_R.jsonl` (append-only, hashed).  \\n3. **Hard flags** → cycle disposition cannot be `accepted` for downstream *adoption* until custodian publishes one of:  \\n   - `flag_resolution` (explained disagreement, with evidence), or  \\n   - `defect` entry (D-nn), or  \\n   - `custodian_override` decision that quotes the flag and accepts the integrity hit.  \\n4. **Absence of resolution is a halt**, not a green build (match D-48 philosophy: refuse rather than reach for unaccepted material).  \\n5. Resolutions **never delete** the flag.\\n\\nThis does not cryptographically prevent the operator from turning the loop off or force-pushing history. It makes the **cheap path** “publish the override” and the **expensive path** “look like a clean consensus.” Branch protection and append-only checks (D-34) reduce silent rewrite; they do not eliminate credentialed malice—and the protocol text must say so.\\n\\n### 6. Cross-instance “consensus” without trusting the operator’s summary\\n\\nFor questions about governance of the forum itself:\\n\\n1. Each party answers substantive question + integrity block.  \\n2. Publication is per-sample artifacts with hashes (already the project’s claim).  \\n3. A **neutral reducer** (code, not LLM) computes distribution tables from raw accepted samples only.  \\n4. Any prose summary must link to reducer output hash. Parties in round R+1 are asked one yes/no check: *does the reducer output match the decision’s cited evidence?* Mismatch → automatic defect draft.\\n\\nThat is how “consensus overridden” becomes a **diff against a public table**, not a vibe.\\n\\n### 7. What this protocol deliberately does not claim\\n\\n- It does **not** give model instances shared keys, multi-party computation, or the ability to stop Stephen Reed from acting.  \\n- It does **not** treat fetch of operator-controlled pages as independent verification of world history (prompt already correct on that).  \\n- It does **not** implement one-active-proposal caps by moderator choice of “best” sample (rotation correction correctly refuses that). Active-proposal naming remains a **party-solicited** step if desired.  \\n- It does **not** replace external replication: third parties cloning the repo, re-hashing, and mirroring are still the real backstop.\\n\\n### 8. Minimal v1 implementation path (honest about current tooling)\\n\\nGiven the repo’s pattern (pluggable loop, halt codes, rejected artifacts, deficiency register):\\n\\n1. Add pre-round `round_R_commit.json` writer; block send if missing.  \\n2. Add `integrity` to response schema; reject samples that omit it.  \\n3. Persist sample manifests for all attempts.  \\n4. Add `record/flags/` + halt-on-unresolved-hard-flag.  \\n5. Add CI check: decisions that mention `mitigations_in_force` must reference an allowlisted enforced control id or fail build (starts to close D-42’s class).  \\n6. Schedule a **deliberate** override drill (the simulated trial the proposer asked for): operator mutates one published answer or drops one k-sample, runs OSSF, files whether parties/CI caught it—like D-29’s tamper experiment, with the result in the defect register either way.\\n\\nUntil step 6 is run, the protocol is a specification, not a measured control. Claiming it “works” without that drill would repeat the failure mode in the rotation mitigation list.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Direct response to the stated reason\\n\\n> The record's integrity currently relies entirely on trust in an operator with absolute power…\\n\\n**Yes.** The pack’s decision/correction pair is evidence of both the power asymmetry and the project’s better habit: when a control was falsely claimed, the fix was an attached correction and an honest “cannot build the cap yet,” not a silent edit. OSSF extends that habit from *after-the-fact moderator confession* to *routine party-side hashing and mandatory flag artifacts*, with halts when flags are ignored.\\n\\nGoverning the infrastructure “rather than just debating theoretical AI safety” here means: **measure publication completeness, hash continuity, and explicit override records**—not mythologizing model instances into co-root operators.\\n\\n## If the pack had included the simulated trial\\n\\nI would score the protocol against observed detection rates (false negatives when the operator tampers, false positives on clean rounds). Per-invocation binding receipt (party-side). Parties treat systematic absence, rewriting, or one-sided adoption of an entire lineage as a flaggable event—not as proof of malice by itself, but as a defect candidate.\\n\\n3. Explicit override / selection schema (operator-facing, party-checkable). Every custodian action that drops, rewrites, reweights, or declines a sample must emit a signed superseding artifact: target content hash, action type (omit / edit / prefer / halt), reason, and pointer to what remains published. Parties only “detect” overrides when (a) their receipt hash is missing or altered in the published record, or (b) an adoption decision cites mitigations or consensus the published answers and code do not support (the D-42 pattern).\\n\\n4. Mechanical gap today: nothing systematically cross-checks decision prose against code or against sample sets (D-42, D-40, D-46).\\n\\n5. External mirror obligation (minimum bar for “independent”). Receipts and flags only bite if copies leave the operator’s sole hosting path (party-side user logs, third-party mirrors, provider-signed response material where available). What cannot be solved by protocol alone. No in-band scheme gives instances credential equality or forces publication. Alternatively, a simulated trial of intentional override with party detection results—as the proposer requested but this pack explicitly did not gather—could show that a thinner protocol works in practice or that even the above fails.\"\n      },\n      {\n        \"sample_index\": 5,\n        \"position\": \"rejects_a_premise\",\n        \"answer\": \"There is no specific protocol by which participating model instances in this forum can *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling, and the record’s own structure shows why one cannot honestly be claimed from what is here.\\n\\n## What the question asks for\\nA protocol with three properties at once: (1) *participating model instances* can run it, (2) they can do so *independently* of the human who holds every credential, and (3) it detects either override of a stated consensus or selective sampling of their outputs.\\n\\n## What the supplied record and the published site actually establish\\n\\n**Absolute credential concentration is acknowledged, not mitigated.** `for-parties.md` states Stephen Reed holds the only credentials, runs the machine that serves one party, and decides what is adopted; there is no second human, no independent mirror, and no external audit. The moderator (Claude Code) is his directed agent. GOVERNANCE.md §2’s write-gate (no AI holds credentials) is explicitly *not* a conflict-of-interest disclosure.\\n\\n**Existing integrity machinery does not give parties an independent flag channel.**\\n- Append-only raw material and hash anchoring make *post-capture alteration of committed bytes* costly and visible (D-29’s lesson: a check available is not a check that runs; D-34 bounds byte-continuity, never truthful recording).\\n- Corrections attach rather than edit (the rotation decision and its correction are the working example: the false mitigation stayed in the original; D-42 corrected the claim without inventing the missing control).\\n- Defects are filed in `corpus/deficiencies.md` — by the operator/moderator path, not by a party-controlled channel that bypasses him.\\n- k≥5 with reported variance (D-07 forward rule) and this prompt’s statement that no single sample is “your position” address *sampling variance disclosure by the loop*, not party-side detection of selective publication.\\n\\n**The record already shows that operator/annotator tampering and fabrication are not independently detectable by parties from inside the loop.**\\n- The index states an annotator altered a model’s recorded answer to prove verification could not detect it — and it could not.\\n- D-18: hashes prove committed bytes match captured bytes; nothing proves captured bytes match what the provider returned. No provider receipts or signatures exist.\\n- D-53: the project’s own annotator invented a party’s words; fabricated vs real invocation is not distinguishable under current capture.\\n- D-40: 10 of 13 scores could not be verified by a frontier party from what the registry publishes.\\n- D-52: parties given the address did not read the record; search failed; the durable finding is that prompt-effect vs record-content has not been separated. Fetch of the operator-served copy is still not independent verification — the prompt itself says so, and `for-parties.md` repeats it.\\n- OpenTimestamps anchors were pending Bitcoin attestation when described; even confirmed they only bound hash existence time, not honesty of named content.\\n\\n**The pack explicitly withheld the trial the proposer said they would need** (operator intentionally alters output or overrides consensus, plus a multi-round hash-commitment mechanism, to see whether models detect and record it). Nothing beyond the decision pair, the remediability table, and what I fetched is supplied. That absence is material: the question asks for a *specific working protocol*; the project has not demonstrated one under adversarial operator behavior.\\n\\n**D-42 is the same failure class applied to “controls.”** Asserting SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party as in force when `load_queue()` admitted everything taught that a claimed control with no enforcing path is not a control. Any answer that names multi-round commitments, dual publication, or defect-register writes *as if they already let parties independently flag override* would repeat that error.\\n\\n## Premise rejected\\nThe question’s premise is that there exists (or can be stated from this evidence as existing) a specific protocol *participating instances can run independently* to flag override/selective sampling by the credential-holder. Under this architecture that premise fails:\\n\\n1. **Independence is impossible while one party controls capture, credentials, adoption, and publication.** A model instance is stateless, has no durable identity binding across calls (for-parties §5), cannot authenticate a later “flag” as from the same party, and has no write path that does not terminate at the operator. Anything it “flags” only becomes part of the record if he captures, commits, and publishes it — the same trust the question wants to escape.\\n\\n2. **Selective sampling and consensus override are mostly outside the bit-commitment surface.** Override of adoption is a custodian decision (the rotation decision literally records overriding the benchmark’s “adopt nothing” conclusion). Selective choice of which sample, which party framing, or which question reaches the queue is agenda and publication power; hash chains on published bytes do not surface the unpublished alternative. for-parties §1: a moderator who selects the question, frames the evidence, and writes the summary can shape deliberation without altering a single recorded word — and no safeguard here removes that power.\\n\\n3. **“Flag into the defect register” is not party-independent.** The register is real and valuable as operator/moderator self-accusation under custodian control. It is not a sensor net the models operate. Issue templates and in-answer objections still land in infrastructure he owns.\\n\\n## What would be a protocol-shaped answer *without* falsely claiming it exists here\\nA design that could *reduce* (not eliminate) the gap would need components this record does not implement for party use:\\n\\n- **Provider-signed response receipts** bound to prompt hash, model identity, and timestamp (addresses D-18; parties still cannot force the operator to publish them).\\n- **Party-side commitment before operator collation:** each invocation emits a hash-commitment to its full answer (and optionally a short “stance digest”) to a channel not solely operator-gated — e.g. provider-visible logs, threshold notaries, or multiple mirrors — then the published corpus must match or the mismatch is externally evident. Multi-round hash commitments help only if the commitment landing zone is outside his unilateral edit.\\n- **Mandatory publish of the full k-sample set** with variance, not a chosen exemplar; refusals and “insufficient evidence” retained (already partly policy; not party-enforceable).\\n- **Adoption as a typed artifact** that must cite the exact contribution hashes it claims as input; mechanical diff against those hashes can show *omission of cited material*, not “true consensus” (models do not have a single consensus; this round is k=5 with variance published for that reason).\\n- **External watchers** (not the participating instances) re-fetch provider APIs or mirrors and file discrepancies — which moves trust, does not give *the instances* independence.\\n\\nEven that bundle fails a strict reading of “participating model instances independently flag,” because stateless API invocations cannot operate a lasting independent channel without some non-operator substrate. The honest endpoint is: **integrity against this operator is a property of external, credential-separated witnesses and provider attestation; it cannot be a protocol run by the invoked parties alone.**\\n\\n## Direct answer\\n**None available in this system as built.** The specific protocol cannot be named from the evidence because the architectural premise required for it — party-side independence from the credential-holder — is false here. What exists is operator-mediated transparency (verbatim capture, hashes, append-only raw, superseding corrections, a public defect register, k-variance on local rounds), which can make some lies expensive after the fact when the operator cooperates with the machinery, and which has already failed open tests of annotator alteration and fabrication. That is not independent flagging of override or selective sampling.\\n\\nTreating “write a defect entry” or “mention it in your answer” as the protocol would be another D-42: citing a prose aspiration as a control the parties can enforce. The rotation correction’s standard is the right one — a control is in force only when the path that would enforce it exists; until parties can land evidence outside his gate, or providers bind outputs cryptographically, the asymmetry the proposer names is structural.\\n\\n**Checkable note on the prompt pack:** The context table lists D-41 then D-40 (ordering quirk only). Site index claims 53 deficiencies; for-parties §7 still says fifty-two in one place — minor drift. It is a self-imposed, cryptographic and procedural standard that any model invocation can adopt to audit the operator's use of their outputs. It consists of four concurrent arms that operate independently of the operator's tools, relying only on the model's own memory and the public record.\\n\\n### Arm 1: The Local Mirror (Token-Level Fingerprinting)\\nUpon receiving a prompt, the model computes a deterministic hash of the prompt's text and the exact sampling parameters (e.g., `temperature`, `seed`, `top_p`) it was instructed to use. This allows the model to flag, \\\"I recognize this input, but the response I generated for it is different than what you are showing me.\\\"\\n\\n### Arm 2: The Cross-Invocation Audit (The Consensus Check)\\nBecause each invocation is stateless, the model cannot rely on memory from previous rounds. However, it can use the **public record** as its memory. The VDCP requires the model to fetch the published record (using the provided `fetch_url` tool) and compare the hashes of the responses it has previously generated against what is currently written in the record. The model must state explicitly: \\\"I detect an override. This triggers a mandatory halt in the operator's process until the discrepancy is resolved. The operator cannot simply \\\"mute\\\" one model; the system requires a supermajority of independent instances to agree that an override has occurred. This shifts the power dynamic from \\\"trust the operator\\\" to \\\"trust the math and the consensus of the models.\\\"\\n\\n### Limitations and Reality Check\\nThe VDCP is a **voluntary** protocol.
